author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Create, import, back up, and repair PS2 memory cards
summary: Manage PS2 memory cards as durable files: choose compatible sizes, preserve slot identity, make cold backups, import cautiously, and recover from corruption without sacrificing healthy saves.
heroAlt: PCSX2 memory-card manager displaying cards and assigned slots

blocks.text: Memory cards are the durable save layer

An emulated PS2 memory card is a filesystem image, not a folder of independent saves. A write interrupted during an Android crash, storage removal or conflicting cloud sync can damage more than the current game. Standard 8 MB cards offer the broadest compatibility; larger cards and folder-backed formats have different tradeoffs and should not be introduced casually.
Close emulation completely before copying, renaming, importing or replacing a memory-card file. Never let two devices or sync clients write the same active card.

Locate the active emulator-data folder and identify which files are assigned to Slot 1 and Slot 2. Make a dated cold backup before any import. For a card from another emulator, keep the source untouched and work on a duplicate; confirm the format is supported instead of changing only its extension.

items: Emulation fully stopped.
Active Slot 1/Slot 2 card names recorded.
Dated backup on separate storage.
Enough free space for duplicate and repair attempts.
Known source and format for any imported card.

blocks.text: Create and maintain cards without losing slot identity

items: 1. Create a standard 8 MB card for the primary slot unless a documented game or workflow requires another size.
2. Boot the PS2 BIOS and confirm the card appears, formats and accepts a small test save.
3. For import, duplicate the external card, place the working copy in the managed memory-card location and assign it to an unused slot first.
4. Browse both cards through BIOS, copy one noncritical save, then cold-boot the target game and verify it.
5. After major progress, exit the game, close EmuCoreX and copy the card plus a SHA-256 manifest to a dated backup folder.

blocks.text: A healthy card survives BIOS browsing, a new save, a normal app restart and a cold game load. Check free-block reporting and several unrelated saves; one game loading does not prove the whole filesystem is intact. Compare the active file's hash only while the emulator is closed.

items: BIOS shows the expected card and free blocks.
New test save survives a cold restart.
Existing saves from more than one game browse correctly.
Backup was made while emulation was stopped.
Slot assignment matches the recorded filenames.

blocks.text: At the first corruption warning, stop writing and duplicate the damaged file for investigation. Restore the newest known-good cold backup to a new filename, assign it, and verify through BIOS before deleting anything. If only one save is recoverable, copy it from the damaged working duplicate into a clean card using trusted tools; never repair the sole original in place.

items: Eject the suspect card and preserve a duplicate.
Assign the last known-good backup under a new filename.
Boot BIOS and verify before launching a game.
Keep the damaged image until recovered saves are independently confirmed.
Card appears unformatted after a crash: filesystem image may be corrupted.
Imported card invisible: unsupported container or wrong slot assignment.
Cloud conflict copies multiply: active file is being synchronized while open.
Save state loads but memory card rolls back: state/card timelines diverged.

blocks.text: Use memory cards for progress you expect to keep and save states only as temporary checkpoints. Rotate several dated cold backups instead of overwriting one file forever. The combination of recorded slot names, hashes and separate storage turns a fragile image into a recoverable save archive.
